body.p: As of the pending Office Action, claims 1-31 are pending and stand rejected. Claims 3, 4, 24, 25, and 27 are amended herein. Claims 32-34 are newly added. No new matter is being added.

By making these amendments, Applicant is not conceding that the claims originally presented were not patentable over the cited references. Applicant reserves the right to pursue patentability of the original claims and/or any other claims supported by the present application in one or more continuing applications.
Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the application in view of the foregoing amendments and the remarks appearing below.
Claims 1-5, 7-9, 12-14, 16, 17, 21 and 24 stand rejected under the judicially created
doctrine of obviousness-type double patenting as being unpatentable over claims 1, 2, 5-7, 10, 13, 21 28 and 29 of U.S. Patent No. 11,206,992.

Without conceding to the rejection and solely to expedite prosecution, Applicant submits herewith a Terminal Disclaimer directed to U.S. Patent No. 11,206,992. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests the rejection be withdrawn.
The Office Action asserts an objection to claim 27. Claim 27 has been amended to overcome the objection. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the present objection.
Rejections Based on 35 U.S.C. 4 112

Claims 23 and 25-27 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (b) as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventors regard as the invention. These rejections are respectfully traversed.

With respect to claim 23, relative terminology as used is not per se indefinite as appears to be suggested in the rejection. As stated in MPEP 2173.05: "Acceptability of [relative terminology in] the claim language depends on whether one of ordinary skill in the art would understand what is claimed, in light of the specification." In this case, the limitation recited in
claim 23 is explained in depth in specification [0121]. On the basis of this description, a person of ordinary skill would clearly understand what is claimed.
Regarding claim 25, the language objected to has been deleted thus mooting this rejection.

Claims 1-5, 7-9, 12, 16, 21 and 24-26 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) as allegedly being anticipated by U.S. Patent Publication No. 20060178695 to Decant et al. ("Decant"). Applicant respectfully disagrees with this rejection for the reasons discussed below.

Decant is an example of a vena cava filter, a well-known, well-understood and long-used type of vascular device. The present Applicant was well-aware of vena cava filters prior to and at the time of filing of the present application. Vena cava filters are an example of typical prior art that was generally considered unsuitable for use as a dimension monitoring device, which in part lead to the present invention. Vena cava filters such as Decant were thus described by the present Applicant in an earlier filed application:
As is understood in the art, there is a long history of implantable vena cava filters to catch clots which embolize from the leg veins, catching them and holding them
in the vena cava until they dissolve in the blood flowing past. The widespread
clinical use of such IVC filters demonstrates the safety and feasibility of anchoring an implant in the TVC and provides useful teachings as to how
aggressively TVC anchors may be shaped, how much radial force a device should
exert, how strong the elements should be, etc. However, in spite of the widespread
use of IVC filters over many years, heretofore it has not been suggested that an implant in the TVC could be utilized for purposes of monitoring fluid volume or
TVC dimensions. Moreover, even if a suggestion were made to equip an IVC filter
with a sensor for monitoring vascular dimensions, such filters would be unsuited to the purpose. The anchoring structures used to secure IVC filters constrain the
vessel from natural size and shape changes in response to changes in fluid volume
and would thus limit the usefulness or accuracy of such a device. USP 10,806,428 B2, col. 3, In. 51 - col. 4, In. 2

There are a number of basic features of Decant, which as a vena cava filter are necessary features to perform its filtering function, that both distinguish Decant from the present claims and make it unsuitable and inoperative as a vascular dimension monitoring device that does not impede blood flow through the vessel in which it is implanted. Decant, as a vascular filter, by design obstructs flow using its legs to form "filter baskets" in order to capture particles in the bloodstream. Rather than teaching an open center, Decant teaches exactly the opposite,

Moreover, the goal of the Decant disclosure is not to change the function of vena cava filters in any way, but to instead provide "a mechanism and/or a sensor for monitoring the condition of the implanted vessel filter." Decant, [0009]. Decant, in the same paragraph, goes on to explain the advantages of such a device:
A device that can provide efficient and cost-effective verification of the condition
of the implanted vessel filter will improve the physicians confidence in the
implanted device, and also allow the physician to intervene when the vessel
[filter, sic.] becomes dislodged through migration or when too much thrombus has
been captured within the vessel filter.

Turning to the specific limitations of the rejected claims, it is clear that the rejections are based on a misunderstanding of the Decant disclosure. Regarding claims 1, 12 and 16, the rejection states that Decant discloses a vessel monitoring device and cites to the Decant Abstract. This is clearly erroneous. The Abstract, as well as numerous other places in the Decant disclosure, stated that the disclosure is directed to a filter with "sensing capability for monitoring the condition of the vessel filter." Decant discloses a filter monitoring device, not a vessel monitoring device.

The rejection next states that Decant discloses a variable inductance coil as recited in claim 1 by pointing to the individual legs 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 and 20 and the conductive bridges that electrically connect alternating legs. This statement is clearly erroneous for a number of reasons. First, it completely ignores the plain meaning of "inductance coil." A coil is well- understood to comprise a series of connected spirals or concentric rings formed by gathering or winding. A further, commonly understood, plain meaning of a coil in an electrical context as used in claim 1 is as a wound spiral of two or more turns of insulated wire, used to introduce inductance into a circuit. See, e.g. https://www.thefreedictionary.com/coil. See also, Stauffer, H. Brooke (2002). NFPA's Pocket Dictionary of Electrical Terms. Jones and Hymel Tucker. p. 36. ISBN 978-0877655992 ("Coil: (1) Conductor wound in a series of convolutions. (2) Successive turns of insulated wire that create a magnetic field when energized. (3) Inductor.").
The legs of the vena cava filter, even when alternating legs are connected by conductors, cannot under any reasonable definition be considered an inductance coil.

While the legs of the Decant vena cava filter do not form an inductance coil, there are, in fact, inductance coils included in the Decant disclosure. The electrical circuits depicted in FIGS. 8A and 8B both include coils 90, 104, 118, 120 for inductive power transfer and reporting of sensed state of the individual legs of the filter. See [0066]-[0071]. The fact that Decant actually discloses coils and describes the coils as consistent with the well-understood plain meaning of the term is a further reason that a person skilled in the art would not consider the legs of the Decant filter to be a coil as asserted in the rejection.

The rejection further asserts that a portion of the Decant device, i.e. the legs from about the middle to the hooked ends, form an open center as claimed. This is not a proper basis for an anticipation rejection based on Decant. Earlier in the explanation of the rejection, it is stated that the legs form the coil, but the legs all converge together at the head of the device to form the closed filter basket. The legs are not a coil and do not create a coil, but if they did, it could not be an open center coil when the legs all converge and are joined at the head of the device. Where inductance coils are identified on the Decant devices it is always at the head of the device, in the very center of the flow obstruction. See, e.g., 104 in FIGS. 9A and 9B.
The rejection also asserts, without basis in the Decant disclosure, that the legs of the

disclosed vena cava filter "move with the vessel wall in response to expansion and collapse of the vessel". The rejection cites to Decant [0053] for support, but this is not what is disclosed there. All that [0053] says is that the legs are flexible or semi-flexible wire so that they can detect strain in the legs that may be induced by trapping of a thrombus in the filter. If the filter legs deformed simply from naturally occurring expansion and collapse of the vessel, that deformation would be falsely interpreted as strain and the entire purpose of the sensing mechanism would be defeated. Sensing movement of the vessel wall with the legs of the vena cava filter is thus actually taught away from by Decant.

The capacitance that the rejection asserts meets the capacitance recited in claim 1 is the capacitor 112 and parasitic capacitance Cp 1 and Cp2 associated with the actual coils 118 and 120 disclosed in the electrical circuit of FIG. 8B. These are not the legs, which are disclosed as including in each a variable resistance 114, 116 to measure strain in the individual legs. It is also noted in the rejection that an apparent basis for the rejection is "'strain or distension' being

a parameter that is 'correlated' to a diameter or area." This is clearly not the disclosure of Decant. Decant is explicit throughout that the "strain or distension" is correlated to the capture of thrombus or particles in the filter basket. See, e.g., [0019], [0056], [0073]. If strain or distension were additionally related to changes in vessel dimension, there would be no way of discriminating between signals induced by the change in dimension versus the capture of thrombus and the purpose of the device would be defeated. Decant does not anticipate the inventions recited in claims 1, 12 and 16 for these reasons.
Regarding claim 2, once again, there is no reasonable, commonly-understood, plain

meaning of the term inductance coil that can be met by the legs of the vena cava filters disclosed in Decant, FIG. 1A or elsewhere. FIG. 1A does not even disclose a continuous single wire around the periphery of the device. As described in [0055] the conductive bridges attach adjacent filter legs so as to form pairs of legs configured with a corresponding measurement circuit as shown in FIG. 1B.

Claim 3 is amended herein to clarify that the capacitance is provided entirely by the inherent capacitance as recited, without a discrete capacitor included in the circuit. This embodiment is disclosed in the present application at [0068]. There is no such disclosure in Decant.

Regarding claim 7, the rejection states that the recited outer layer covering the plurality of wire strands is the sleeve 6, clearly located only at the head of the device, i.e. in the center, as shown in FIG. 1B. Sleeve 6 only covers a small part of the legs where it joins them together, and sleeve 6 is positioned directly in the middle of the device that is asserted to have an open center in the rejection of claim 1. This rejection is made in error for this further reason.

Regarding claims 8 and 9, the rejection changes its explanation of conductive bridges 26 from being part of the coil in claim 1, to now forming the recited sensor frame formed in an open center loop. Conductive bridges 26 cannot be both the coil and the frame supporting the coil. Conductive bridges 26 are also not disclosed as being provided in a complete loop with an open center but are instead just short segments electrically joining pairs of legs to form a sensing circuit. [0055] and [0056] do not support the assertion that conductive bridges 26 are formed in a loop surrounding an inner periphery of the vessel when implanted. All that is said in those paragraphs is that conductive bridges 26 electrically connect adjacent legs to form electrical
circuits including pairs of legs. The rejection of claims 8 and 9 is thus made in error for these further reasons.

Claim 24 is amended herein to refer to a body lumen as described in application [0176]. It is further amended to clarify the structure of the recited coil. Decant does not show or suggest a coil as claimed with multiple wire strands wrapped together in a loop with adjacent wire strands lying in contact along their length. Claim 24 and its dependent claims are thus patentable over the cited reference.
Claim 27 is amended herein to clarify that the device capacitance consists essentially of the inherent capacitance. This feature is not disclosed in Decant.

New claims 32, 33 and 34 are added dependent on claim 25 to further define features of the claimed coil as described, for example, in [0075] and [0145] of the present application. These structures are also not shown or suggested in Decant.

Claims 5, 10, 11, 17-20 and 30 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Decant in view of U.S. Publication No. 20170216508 to Zilbershlag et al. ("Zilbershlag"). This rejection is respectfully traversed.

Claim 5 is rejected on the basis that the addition of insulation to the filter legs of Decant is suggested by the teachings of Zilbershlag "because doing so would help make the device biocompatible, as recognized by Zilbershlag [0151]." This is not a correct statement of the teachings of Zilbershlag, which states only that "[t]he covering is preferably bio compatible and provides insulation." There is nothing stated about the purpose of the covering being to increase the overall biocompatibility of the device. The biocompatibility of the covering material is simply stated as a requirement in the selection of the material, not as a feature improving the overall biocompatibility of the device as a whole. Decant discloses the legs of its device without mentioning any coverings or insulation except at the sleeve 6. Biocompatible covering materials such as identified in Zilbershlag were well-known from prior to the filing of Decant. Decant chose not to suggest the use of such known coverings. The fact that Zilbershlag in 2017
acknowledges the existence of such materials does not teach a person of ordinary skill to modify Decant.

The modification of Decant to meet the limitations of claim 10 is not understood. The individual legs of Decant are configured specifically to form a filter basket to capture thrombus and other particles in the bloodstream. There is nothing in Zilbershlag, which discloses inductive power coupling devices, to suggest altering the filter forming legs of Decant. Moreover, Decant already discloses inductive power coupling coils, e.g. coils 90 and 104 in FIG. 8A. To the extent any teachings of Zilbershlag may be relevant to Decant, it is with respect to the power coupling coils of Decant, which otherwise do not meet the limitations of claim 9 as explained above.
The rejection of claims 11, 17-20 and 30 are also made in error for the reasons explained with respect to both claims 5 and 10 above.
Claims 6 and 22 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Decant in view of U.S. Patent No. 3838683 to Kolin ("Kolin"). This rejection is respectfully traversed.

Kolin describes a catheter with a flow meter on the distal end. Decant is an implanted vena cava filter with no need or purpose for a flow meter. The purpose of the configuration of Kolin pointed to in the rejection is to allow the flow meter to be introduced into and effective in measuring flow in different size and shape vessels. The Decant vena cava filter goes in one place - the vena cava. The individual legs of the Decant vena cava filter allow it to engage the wall of the vena cava effective for its specific purpose of filtering out thrombus or other particles in the blood stream. Moreover, the Decant filter is a small device specifically configured to be implanted in the vena cava. [0006] of Decant describes the process and device for delivering vena cava filters - specifically that the filters are designed for compression into a small size to facilitate delivery. Modifying the device to make it flexible as suggested by Kolin would provide no advantage in delivering the vena cava filter.
There is no basis in the cited references for the proposed combination. This rejection is based entirely on hindsight in an attempt to find claim limitations that are not shown or taught as claimed.
Claims 13-15, 29 and 31 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Decant in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 20080033527 to Nunez et al. ("Nunez").

The rejection of claim 12 is based on the assertion that the legs 4 and conductive bridges 26 of Decant form the recited coil. The proposed modification of Decant to meet the limitations of claim 13-15 would then require that the legs of the vena cava filter be wrapped onto a frame. The legs of Decant are straight and specifically configured for the purpose of forming a filter basket to capture particles and to sense the capture of particle as a result of strain induced in the legs when particles are captured. [0056]. The supposed motivation to "predictably help the device be suitable for implanting within an injured or diseased blood vessel, as recognized by Nunez" makes no sense because the purpose of Decant is not to repair injured or diseased vessels. The purpose of Decant is to filter blood irrespective of the health of the vessel in which it is placed.
The rejection of claims 29 and 31 is also made in error for these same reasons, as well as the reasons stated above with respect to claims 1, 12 and 16.
Claims 27 and 28 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Decant in view of PCT Publication No. W02006125215 to Gray et al. ("Gray"). This rejection is respectfully traversed.
First, Gray is not analogous art. It is an electromagnetic resonant circuit sleave to

facilitate magnetic resonance imaging within an implanted stent. It is not from the same field of endeavor as the present invention and teaches nothing of relevance to the problems solved by the present invention. The rejection is made in error for this reason alone.
Regarding claim 27, neither Decant nor Gray, nor the combination of the references
teaches or suggest that the inherent capacitance be the only source of capacitance as now recited in amended claim 27.

Regarding claim 28, first as explained previously, Decant does not disclose the claimed coil. However, the proposed modification of Decant also makes no sense. The wire strands of the supposed coil in Decant comprise the individual legs of the device. They are already connected together at one end, or in some embodiments at both ends. As can be seen in Decant, when the ends of the legs are connected together, they still do not form a loop. However, as shown in Gray FIG. 9, the ends referred to in [0077] do not actually touch each other but

instead are separated by a gap to form a capacitor. It is not clear why a person skilled in the art would want to form such a capacitor in Decant, but if they did, then without the ends in contact there would be no variable inductance coil formed by the loop thus configured. This rejection is thus made in error for this additional reason.

allowance thereof is respectfully requested. Applicant's amendment of the claims does not constitute a concession that the claims are not allowable in their unamended form.
